topic: Changes of state and the particle model
subject: physics

items.q: How is the density of a material defined?
items.correct: The mass of the material divided by its volume.
items.misconception: The volume of the material divided by its mass.
items.why: Dividing a small number into a large one feels wrong to students, and awkward decimals such as 0.0025 encourage them to flip the calculation so the arithmetic looks friendlier. Anchor the order to the unit. Density is in kilograms per metre cubed, and 'per' means divided by, so kilograms go on top and metres cubed underneath. The unit tells you the order every time.
items.random_wrong: The mass of the material multiplied by its volume.

items.q: A liquid has a density of 800 kg/m³ and a mass of 2.0 kg. What is its volume?
items.misconception: 400 m³
items.why: Dividing a small number into a large one feels wrong to students, and awkward decimals such as 0.0025 encourage them to flip the calculation so the arithmetic looks friendlier. Anchor the order to the unit. Density is in kilograms per metre cubed, and 'per' means divided by, so kilograms go on top and metres cubed underneath. The unit tells you the order every time.

items.q: Which unit does the specification use for density?
items.correct: kg/m³
items.misconception: g/cm³
items.why: Students see unit changes as relabelling rather than rescaling, and because both unit strings contain a mass unit over a volume unit the two look equivalent at a glance. Use water as the check. Water is 1.0 g/cm³ and 1000 kg/m³, and the same substance cannot have two different numbers unless the unit changes the scale.

items.q: A solid cube of side 0.20 m has a mass of 54 kg. What is its density?
items.correct: 6750 kg/m³
items.misconception: 270 kg/m³
items.why: The measured quantity is a length, so it is the number students reach for. Working in three dimensions is an extra step that is easy to drop, especially when the side length is less than one and cubing makes the number smaller. Label every number with its unit before dividing. Only m³ underneath gives kg/m³ on top; dividing by a length gives kg/m, which is not a density.

items.q: Aluminium has a density of 2.7 g/cm³. What is this in kg/m³?
items.correct: 2700 kg/m³
items.why: Only the mass part of the unit is converted. The cubic centimetre to cubic metre step is invisible, and it is the larger factor of the two. Convert both parts. 1 g = 0.001 kg and 1 cm³ = 0.000001 m³, so 1 g/cm³ = 0.001 / 0.000001 = 1000 kg/m³. Sense-check the size: aluminium at 0.0027 kg/m³ would be lighter than air.

items.q: Which description matches a correct simple particle diagram of a solid?
items.correct: Particles touching each other in a regular, ordered pattern.
items.misconception: Particles evenly spaced in a grid, with gaps in between them.
items.why: Students draw a lattice to show order and leave gaps so the pattern is easy to see. The gaps then get read as a physical feature of the solid. Marking a diagram of a solid requires the particles to be touching as well as regular. Order and close packing are two separate points, and both must appear.
items.random_wrong: Particles touching one another but jumbled, not in a pattern.

items.q: Why is the density of a gas far lower than the density of the same substance as a liquid?
items.correct: The same particles are spread through a much larger volume.
items.misconception: The particles in a gas are lighter than those in a liquid.
items.why: Density is being explained by a property of the individual particle rather than by their spacing, which is the only thing the particle model actually changes between states. Ask where the extra particles would have gone. Boil 1 kg of water and you get 1 kg of steam, made of exactly the same molecules; only the volume has changed.
items.random_wrong: Each particle grows bigger when the liquid becomes a gas.

items.q: A block of solid wax melts. The mass does not change, but the liquid wax takes up slightly more volume. What happens to the density?
items.correct: It falls slightly, because the particles are a little further apart.
items.misconception: It falls a long way, because liquid particles are far apart.
items.why: Textbook diagrams often exaggerate the gaps in liquids to show that the particles can move, and the sequence solid, liquid, gas suggests spacing increases in equal steps. Compare real values: ice is about 920 kg/m³, water 1000 kg/m³, steam about 0.6 kg/m³. The huge jump comes at boiling, which tells you the big change in spacing happens there.
items.random_wrong: It stays the same, because exactly the same particles are present.

items.q: A student is finding the density of a rectangular metal block. Which measurements are needed?
items.correct: The mass on a balance, and the length, width and height.
items.misconception: The mass on a balance, and the area of its largest face.
items.why: The measured quantity is a length, so it is the number students reach for. Working in three dimensions is an extra step that is easy to drop, especially when the side length is less than one and cubing makes the number smaller. Label every number with its unit before dividing. Only m³ underneath gives kg/m³ on top; dividing by a length gives kg/m, which is not a density.
items.random_wrong: The weight in newtons, and the length, width and height.

items.q: A measuring cylinder contains 40 cm³ of water. A stone of mass 60 g is lowered in and the level rises to 65 cm³. What is the density of the stone?
items.correct: 2.4 g/cm³
items.misconception: 0.92 g/cm³
items.why: The final reading is the number the student has just read, and it feels like the answer. The starting volume of water is treated as part of the apparatus rather than as part of the measurement. Always record both readings and subtract. The water that was already there has not become part of the stone.

items.q: An empty measuring cylinder has a mass of 85 g. It is filled to the 50 cm³ mark with oil and the total mass is 129 g. What is the density of the oil?
items.correct: 0.88 g/cm³
items.misconception: 2.58 g/cm³
items.why: The balance reading is taken as the mass of the liquid. Once the cylinder is on the balance it stops being seen as an object with a mass of its own. Either subtract the mass of the empty cylinder or zero (tare) the balance with the empty cylinder on it. Sense-check the answer: an oil of 2.6 g/cm³ would be denser than glass.

items.q: Which apparatus is most suitable for measuring the diameter of a copper wire about 0.4 mm across?
items.correct: A micrometer, which has a resolution of about 0.01 mm.
items.misconception: A ruler, because 0.4 mm can be judged between the marks.
items.why: Rulers are the familiar instrument and estimating between marks feels like good practice. The idea that an instrument has a resolution, and that the measurement is worthless below it, is newer and less concrete. Compare the resolution with the measurement. An uncertainty of about 0.5 mm on a 0.4 mm diameter is larger than the quantity being measured; with a micrometer it is around 1 per cent.
items.random_wrong: Any of the three, since they all measure a length in mm.

items.q: A 200 g block of ice melts completely inside a sealed container. What is the mass of the water formed?
items.correct: 200 g, because exactly the same particles are still there.
items.misconception: Less than 200 g, because some of the ice is used up in melting.
items.why: The balance provides direct evidence that seems to settle the question, and a gas that disperses invisibly stops feeling like a substance at all. Follow the particles, not the balance. Repeat the change in a sealed container and the reading does not change, because nothing has left the system.
items.random_wrong: More than 200 g, because the water is denser than the ice was.

items.q: Water is boiled away in an open pan standing on a balance, and the reading falls. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The steam has carried the mass out of the pan; none is lost.
items.misconception: The mass has been destroyed by the heat from the hotplate.
items.why: The balance provides direct evidence that seems to settle the question, and a gas that disperses invisibly stops feeling like a substance at all. Follow the particles, not the balance. Repeat the change in a sealed container and the reading does not change, because nothing has left the system.
items.random_wrong: The water has become steam, and a gas has no mass at all.

items.q: Why is boiling water classed as a physical change rather than a chemical change?
items.correct: Cooling the steam gives back water with its original properties.
items.misconception: Steam is a new substance, but the water can be made again.
items.why: A change in appearance is read as a change of substance, and the three states are often given different names, which makes them sound like different materials. Apply the specification's test: reverse the change and see whether the original properties come back. Condense the steam and it is water again, so nothing new was made.
items.random_wrong: Reversing it is possible, and chemical changes are never reversible.

items.q: Solid carbon dioxide sublimates in an open dish on a balance and the reading falls. Which explanation is correct?
items.correct: The gas has left the dish, so the mass of it all is unchanged.
items.misconception: The solid has been used up, so that mass no longer exists.
items.why: The balance provides direct evidence that seems to settle the question, and a gas that disperses invisibly stops feeling like a substance at all. Follow the particles, not the balance. Repeat the change in a sealed container and the reading does not change, because nothing has left the system.
items.random_wrong: A chemical reaction has turned the solid into a new gas.

items.q: A 2 kg block of aluminium is cut exactly in half. What is the density of each half?
items.correct: The same, because the mass and the volume both halve.
items.misconception: Half, because each piece now has only half of the mass.
items.why: Density is met through the equation, and the equation contains mass, which obviously halves. Students track the numerator and forget that the denominator halves at the same time. Work the numbers through: if m and V both halve, m / V is unchanged. Reinforce that every piece of a pure material, however small, has the same density.
items.random_wrong: Half, because each piece is lighter than the whole block.

items.q: A large lump of expanded polystyrene has a bigger mass than a small steel ball bearing. Which has the greater density?
items.correct: The steel. Density is mass per unit volume, not mass on its own. The steel packs far more mass into each cubic metre, so its density is about 7800 kg/m³ against roughly 20 kg/m³ for the polystyrene.
items.misconception: The polystyrene, because it is heavier - the heavier object must be the denser one.
items.why: In everyday speech 'heavy' and 'dense' are used interchangeably, and students meet mass long before they meet density. Comparing two objects of very different sizes hides the fact that density is a ratio, so only the top of the ratio is noticed. Always compare equal volumes. Ask which would be heavier: a cubic centimetre of steel or a cubic centimetre of polystyrene. Once the volume is fixed, the comparison of mass is a comparison of density.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the density of a 3.0 kg block of volume 0.0020 m³ found by multiplying or dividing?
items.correct: By dividing: 3.0 / 0.0020 = 1500 kg/m³. The equation is ρ = m/V.
items.misconception: You multiply mass by volume, because a bigger object with a bigger volume must have more density in it.
items.why: Students who half-remember the equation reach for multiplication because it is easier, and because 'more stuff means more density' sounds reasonable when density and amount have not been separated. Check the answer against the unit and against a known material. Multiplying gives a number in kg m³, which is not a density unit at all, and gives water a value nothing like 1000 kg/m³.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A student measures a block with a newton-meter and records 5.9 N. Can that value be used in ρ = m/V?
items.correct: No. The equation needs mass in kilograms, measured on a balance. The 5.9 N is a weight, which is a force in newtons.
items.misconception: Mass and weight are the same thing, so a reading in newtons can go straight into the density equation.
items.why: Everyday language uses 'weight' for what a balance shows, and both quantities increase together for a given object, so the distinction feels like fussy vocabulary rather than a real difference. The specification is explicit: mass, m, in kilograms, kg. A newton-meter measures force. Insist on a balance for mass, and keep newtons out of ρ = m/V.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When ice melts to water, do the water molecules become bigger?
items.correct: No. The molecules are unchanged. What changes is how they are arranged and how they move; the same molecules occupy a slightly different volume.
items.misconception: Particles swell up when a substance melts or boils, and that is why a gas takes up so much more room than a liquid.
items.why: Diagrams of a gas often use larger or more spread-out circles, and everyday talk of things 'expanding' is applied to the particles themselves rather than to the spaces between them. Draw all three states with identical circles and change only the spacing and pattern. Expansion is extra space between particles, never bigger particles.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a substance always denser as a solid than as a liquid?
items.correct: For most substances, yes, because the particles pack slightly more closely in the solid. Water is the well-known exception: ice floats because its molecules are held in a more open arrangement than in liquid water, so ice is less dense.
items.misconception: The solid form of any substance must be denser than the liquid, so ice ought to sink in water.
items.why: The rule that solids are denser than liquids is learned as absolute, and the everyday sight of floating ice is filed away separately instead of being used to test the rule. Keep the explanation in terms of arrangement. Density follows from how closely the particles are packed, and in ice the arrangement is more open than in liquid water, so the usual order is reversed.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does it matter which length-measuring instrument is used, as long as it reads in millimetres?
items.correct: Yes. A ruler, Vernier callipers and a micrometer resolve to roughly 1 mm, 0.1 mm and 0.01 mm, so the choice must suit the size of the dimension being measured.
items.misconception: Any instrument will do, because they all measure length in the same unit and so give the same answer.
items.why: Instruments are grouped by what they measure rather than by how finely they measure it, and the unit on the scale is mistaken for the precision of the reading. Set the instrument against the object. Use a ruler for a block of a few centimetres, callipers for smaller objects, and a micrometer for a wire or a thin sheet.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A sealed bottle of water is put in a freezer. Does its mass change as the water freezes?
items.correct: No. Mass is conserved in a change of state. The ice takes up slightly more volume than the water did, so the density falls, but the mass is exactly the same.
items.misconception: The ice must be heavier, because it takes up more room than the water did.
items.why: Volume and mass are not yet separated, so anything that gets bigger is assumed to have gained matter. Freezing water is the everyday example where the two clearly come apart. Keep mass and volume separate. Freezing changes only the arrangement of the molecules, so V goes up, m stays the same and ρ = m/V goes down.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does the water vapour that leaves a puddle have any mass?
items.correct: Yes. A gas is made of the same particles as the liquid, so it has mass. Weighing a sealed flask before and after a liquid evaporates inside it shows no change.
items.misconception: Gases have no mass at all - you cannot weigh air, and steam just floats away.
items.why: Gases are invisible, they rise, and nothing is felt when a hand passes through them, so students treat 'no weight you can feel' as 'no mass'. Point to evidence that gases have mass: a sealed container of an evaporating liquid keeps the same reading throughout, because the particles are still inside it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is every change that can be reversed a physical change?
items.correct: Not necessarily. What makes a change of state physical is that the material recovers its original properties when the change is reversed, so no new substance was ever made.
items.misconception: Physical changes are the reversible ones and chemical changes can never be reversed, so anything reversible must be physical.
items.why: 'Reversible means physical' is an easy rule to remember, and most classroom chemical changes are hard to undo, which appears to confirm it. State the test the way the specification does: the material recovers its original properties if the change is reversed. It is the recovery of the same material, not the mere fact of reversal, that marks the change as physical.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
